position_in_era.historical_role: Stones' first disco-influenced single, knocking Saturday Night Fever soundtrack from US #1 — became the canonical case of a major rock band performing disco's genetic material under rock's stylistic envelope, ahead of Queen's similar pivot two years later.

narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Recorded during Keith Richards' drug-trial distraction — Mick Jagger took unusual artistic control. The 'four-on-the-floor' pulse came from Billy Preston demoing it to Mick at El Mocambo Toronto, March 1977. Bill Wyman went 'to quite a few clubs' (per engineer Chris Kimsey) to dial in the bassline. Keith's resistance to disco is documented but he later said the song 'was a damn good disco record; it was calculated to be one'.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: Studio 54 (1977-1980 NYC) is the song cultural locus. Jagger was a regular. The disco-rock fusion was reverse-imported from Black/queer/Latino dance culture into the white rock elite.
narrative_slots.production_facts: Engineered by Chris Kimsey at Pathe Marconi Studios, Paris. The dry drum sound — what Charlie Watts called Philadelphia-style drumming — was deliberate. The 12-inch single (8+ minutes) was mixed by Bob Clearmountain, Stones first 12-inch.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Harmonica: Sugar Blue (James Whiting), 22-year-old American street musician discovered by Sandy Whitelaw in the Paris Metro. Saxophone: Mel Collins, brought in because Bobby Keys relationship with Jagger was strained.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: Released 19 May 1978 as Some Girls' first single. Hit US #1 on 5 August, ending Andy Gibb's seven-week reign. Stones' eighth and final US number-one. Reached UK #3.
